sections.h2: Selling in Derry Township and Hershey
sections.html:
Derry Township is the municipality that holds Hershey. It lies in southeastern Dauphin County, east of Harrisburg, and a Hershey address usually carries a Derry Township deed. Palmdale, Swatara, Hockersville, Oakmont, Waltonville and part of Stoverdale are also unincorporated communities inside its lines.

The medical center, the children's hospital, the chocolate business and visitor spending support the local economy, and that tends to keep buyers coming. The township had an estimated 25,179 residents on July 1, 2025, barely above the 24,679 counted in 2010. About 63.1 percent of households own their home. An owned home has a midpoint value of $390,000, and midpoint monthly rent is $1,361. Tax bills run through Dauphin County instead of a local collector, so the county is your first stop on paperwork.

sections.h2: Who bills property tax, and at what rates
sections.html:
As of January 1, 2023, the Dauphin County Treasurer's Office bills and collects real estate taxes for both the township and the Derry Township School District. The township's Tax Association Office shut that day, and occupation and local services taxes went to Keystone Collections Group.

Real estate millage, with the transfer tax shares
Levy or shareRate
Derry Township real estate tax2.53810 mills
Derry Township School District real estate tax20.3387 mills
Dauphin County real estate tax9.193 mills
Transfer tax to the state1 percent of the price
Transfer tax to the township0.5 percent of the price
Transfer tax to the school district0.5 percent of the price

Budgets change these rates, so verify them with the county treasurer before you draw up an estimate of your proceeds. Some township levies attach to a person and not a property. The earned income tax is 1 percent, shared equally by the township and the school district, and the township also takes $250 from each working resident who earns over $12,000. Those are the new owner's concern and never reduce what you net.

Expect 2 percent of the price in all. One percent goes to the Department of Revenue, and the municipality and the school district split the remaining one percent evenly. Your sales agreement says who pays, though the state holds both parties liable.

Deeds between spouses, between parents and children, between grandparents and grandchildren and between siblings are generally exempt. Any other exemption should be confirmed with an attorney or the Department of Revenue. Deeds are recorded at the Dauphin County Courthouse in Harrisburg, where records go back to 1785, and the legislature sets recording fees.

Dauphin County's Office of Tax Assessment values real property and keeps ownership records. It also administers the homestead and farmstead exclusion, the Clean and Green program for preferential assessment and a tax deferral program. Find it on the second floor of the County Administration Building, 2 South Second Street, Harrisburg. Parcel data is online.

Tax rates come from the county, the township and the school district after assessments are final, not from this office. If your assessment looks too high, ask for the appeal rules and the filing date that cover your parcel.

Rental owners should know about Act 29 of 2026, which set up a county contact registry for properties without an owner in residence. An owner, or a lender after foreclosure, must supply a name, address, phone number and email for a person who can resolve code violations. The deadline is 30 days after taking ownership and 30 days after any change. A $500 fine applies for noncompliance, and principal residences occupied by their owners are exempt.

Visit the township municipal complex at 600 Clearwater Road in Hershey for questions on permits, zoning and any open code matter at your address. A trip before you list can save time, because buyers and their lenders tend to ask for the same records.

  • Check that earlier projects, such as a finished basement, a deck or a pool, were permitted.
  • Learn the zoning district if a buyer might want a business, an addition or a rental.
  • Make sure street light assessments and other township charges are paid up.
  • Join the township's eNews list for notices about your street.

A well-kept house can sell on the open market. Selling as-is fits better when an estate needs settling, you are relocating, or the repairs are ones you do not want to finance.

Whatever you pick, insist on a written estimate of your proceeds: the price, minus 2 percent transfer tax if you agree to pay it, loan payoffs, prorated county, township and school taxes, and any repair credit. Before you pull the house off the market, ask for the buyer's proof of funds and a firm closing date.

Collect the deed, current county, township and school tax statements, permit records and, if a loan is open, a payoff letter. For an estate sale, add the papers showing who has authority to sign. For a rental, add the lease and rent history.

Find out from the treasurer what, if anything, is unpaid. The title company then settles it out of your sale money. Cash buyers want the same items, but the process moves faster because no lender is waiting on an appraisal.

After you sign a purchase agreement, a title company starts its file and searches the chain of ownership. It will request tax balances from the treasurer and look for anything else recorded against the property. If a defect turns up, such as an old lien or a misspelled owner name, resolving it can take longer than anything else in the sale, so raise any known title question at the start.

On settlement day you sign the deed and the closing statement. The deed is then recorded in Harrisburg. A buyer using a mortgage needs an appraisal and underwriting first, which adds weeks. A cash buyer skips both, so the schedule follows the title search and your own move-out plans. If you need extra days in the house after closing, negotiate that into the agreement before signing.

Whether the buyer is an investor, a family or a company, ask the same short list. Is the offer in writing, and is it contingent on a mortgage, an inspection or the sale of another house? Who pays closing costs and the transfer tax? How long is the buyer willing to wait for you to move? Can the buyer show funds on hand?

Put the answers on paper, then rank offers by the cash that reaches your account, which is the price minus payoffs, prorated taxes and any credits, and not on the headline number alone.

faqs.q: Is Hershey a separate town from Derry Township?
faqs.a: No. Hershey is unincorporated and lies within Derry Township, so a Hershey address means township permits and deeds, and Dauphin County taxes.

faqs.q: What is the transfer tax on a house sale in Derry Township?
faqs.a: Two percent of the price in all. The state gets 1 percent, and the township and school district get 0.5 percent each, collected through the Dauphin County Recorder of Deeds.

faqs.q: Who collects real estate taxes on a Derry Township house?
faqs.a: The Dauphin County Treasurer's Office, for the township and the school district alike. Call for balances before closing.

faqs.q: Do I need to register a rental house I am selling in Dauphin County?
faqs.a: Act 29 of 2026 asks owners of non-owner-occupied property for contact details, updated within 30 days of any change. The buyer takes on that duty at purchase.

faqs.q: Are family transfers exempt from realty transfer tax in Dauphin County?
faqs.a: Deeds among spouses, parents and children, grandparents and grandchildren, and siblings are usually exempt. Other exemptions exist, so ask an attorney or the Department of Revenue.
